One of the sons of Bela ([1 Chr. 7:7](#1Chr.7.7)).
A Benjamite slinger who joined David at Ziklag ([1 Chr. 12:5](#1Chr.12.5)).
A Levite, one of the overseers of the temple offerings ([2 Chr. 31:13](#2Chr.31.13)) in the reign of Hezekiah.

The son of Nebat ([1 Kings 11:26-39](#1Kgs.11.26)), “an Ephrathite,” the first king of the ten tribes, over whom he reigned twenty-two years (B.C. 976-945). He was the son of a widow of Zereda, and while still young was promoted by Solomon to be chief superintendent of the “burnden”, i.e., of the bands of forced labourers. …

Jeroboam II., the son and successor of Jehoash, and the fourteenth king of Israel, over which he ruled for forty-one years, B.C. 825-784 ([2 Kings 14:23](#2Kgs.14.23)). He followed the example of the first Jeroboam in keeping up the worship of the golden calves ([2 Kings 14:24](#2Kgs.14.24)). His reign was contemporary with those of Amaziah ([2 Kings 14:23](#2Kgs.14.23)) and Uzziah (15:1), kings of Judah. …
Father of Elkanah, and grandfather of the prophet Samuel ([1 Sam. 1:1](#1Sam.1.1)).
[1 Chr. 9:12](#1Chr.9.12); a priest, perhaps the same as in [Neh. 11:12](#Neh.11.12).
The father of Azareel, the “captain” of the tribe of Dan ([1 Chr. 27:22](#1Chr.27.22)).
[2 Chr. 23:1](#2Chr.23.1); one whose son assisted in placing Joash on the throne.
Contender with the shame; i.e., idol, a surname also of Gideon ([2 Sam. 11:21](#2Sam.11.21)).
Possession, or possessed; i.e., “by a husband”, the wife of Uzziah, and mother of king Jotham ([2 Kings 15:33](#2Kgs.15.33)).
One of the three sons of Hananiah ([1 Chr. 3:21](#1Chr.3.21)).
A Kohathite Levite, the father of Joram, of the family of Eliezer ([1 Chr. 26:25](#1Chr.26.25)); called also Isshiah (24:21).
One of the sons of Jeduthum ([1 Chr. 25:3](#1Chr.25.3), [15](#1Chr.25.15)).
Upright towards God, the head of the seventh division of Levitical musicians ([1 Chr. 25:14](#1Chr.25.14)).
Seat of his father, the head of the fourteenth division of priests ([1 Chr. 24:13](#1Chr.24.13)).
Uprightness, the first of the three sons of Caleb by Azubah ([1 Chr. 2:18](#1Chr.2.18)).
Head of the ninth priestly order ([Ezra 2:36](#Ezra.2.36)); called also Jeshuah ([1 Chr. 24:11](#1Chr.24.11)).
A Levite appointed by Hezekiah to distribute offerings in the priestly cities ([2 Chr. 31:15](#2Chr.31.15)).

Firm, or a gift, a son of Obed, the son of Boaz and Ruth ([Ruth 4:17](#Ruth.4.17), [22](#Ruth.4.22); [Matt. 1:5](#Matt.1.5), [6](#Matt.1.6); [Luke 3:32](#Luke.3.32)). He was the father of eight sons, the youngest of whom was David ([1 Sam. 17:12](#1Sam.17.12)). The phrase “stem of Jesse” is used for the family of David ([Isa. 11:1](#Isa.11.1)), and “root of Jesse” for the Messiah ([Isa. 11:10](#Isa.11.10); [Rev. 5:5](#Rev.5.5)). Jesse was a man apparently of wealth and position at Bethlehem ([1 Sam. 17:17](#1Sam.17.17), [18](#1Sam.17.18), [20](#1Sam.17.20); [Ps. 78:71](#Ps.78.71)). The last reference to him is of David’s procuring for him an asylum with the king of Moab ([1 Sam. 22:3](#1Sam.22.3)).

Anointed, the Greek translation of the Hebrew word rendered “Messiah” (q.v.), the official title of our Lord, occurring five hundred and fourteen times in the New Testament. It denotes that he was anointed or consecrated to his great redemptive work as Prophet, Priest, and King of his people. He is Jesus the Christ ([Acts 17:3](#Acts.17.3); [18:5](#Acts.18.5); [Matt. 22:42](#Matt.22.42)), the Anointed One. He is thus spoken of by Isaiah (61:1), and by Daniel (9:24-26), who styles him “Messiah the Prince.”
The father of Amasa, David’s general ([1 Kings 2:5](#1Kgs.2.5), [32](#1Kgs.2.32)); called Ithra ([2 Sam. 17:25](#2Sam.17.25)).
The oldest of Gideon’s seventy sons ([Judg. 8:20](#Judg.8.20)).
A peg, or a prince, one of the Edomitish kings of Mount Seir ([Gen. 36:40](#Gen.36.40)).

“The priest of Midian,” Moses’ father-in-law ([Ex. 2:18](#Exod.2.18))=Raguel ([Num. 10:29](#Num.10.29)). If he be identified with Jethro (q.v.), then this may be regarded as his proper name, and Jether or Jethro (i.e., “excellency”) as his official title.
An enclosure, one of the twelve sons of Ishmael ([Gen. 25:15](#Gen.25.15)).
Snatched away by God, a descendant of Zerah ([1 Chr. 9:6](#1Chr.9.6)).
The oldest of Esau’s three sons by Aholibamah ([Gen. 36:5](#Gen.36.5), [14](#Gen.36.14), [18](#Gen.36.18)).
A Levite, one of the sons of Shimei ([1 Chr. 23:10](#1Chr.23.10), [11](#1Chr.23.11)).
A son of Bilhan, grandson of Benjamin ([1 Chr. 7:10](#1Chr.7.10)).
One of the three sons of Rehoboam ([2 Chr. 11:19](#2Chr.11.19)).
A Maachathite ([2 Kings 25:23](#2Kgs.25.23); [Jer. 40:8](#Jer.40.8); [42:1](#Jer.42.1)). He is also called Azariah ([Jer. 43:2](#Jer.43.2)).

Chaste, the daughter of Ethbaal, the king of the Zidonians, and the wife of Ahab, the king of Israel ([1 Kings 16:31](#1Kgs.16.31)). This was the “first time that a king of Israel had allied himself by marriage with a heathen princess; and the alliance was in this case of a peculiarly disastrous kind. Jezebel has stamped her name on history as the representative of all that is designing, crafty, malicious, revengeful, and cruel. …
Assembled by God, a son of Azmaveth. He was one of the Benjamite archers who joined David at Ziklag ([1 Chr. 12:3](#1Chr.12.3)).

One of the three sons of Zeruiah, David’s sister, and “captain of the host” during the whole of David’s reign ([2 Sam. 2:13](#2Sam.2.13); [10:7](#2Sam.10.7); [11:1](#2Sam.11.1); [1 Kings 11:15](#1Kgs.11.15)). His father’s name is nowhere mentioned, although his sepulchre at Bethlehem is mentioned ([2 Sam. 2:32](#2Sam.2.32)). His two brothers were Abishai and Asahel, the swift of foot, who was killed by Abner ([2 Sam. 2:13-32](#2Sam.2.13)), whom Joab afterwards treacherously murdered (3:22-27). He afterwards led the assault at the storming of the fortress on Mount Zion, and for this service was raised to the rank of “prince of the king’s army” ([2 Sam. 5:6-10](#2Sam.5.6); [1 Chr. 27:34](#1Chr.27.34)). His chief military achievements were, (1) against the allied forces of Syria and Ammon; (2) against Edom ([1 Kings 11:15](#1Kgs.11.15), [16](#1Kgs.11.16)); and (3) against the Ammonites ([2 Sam. 10:7-19](#2Sam.10.7); [11:1](#2Sam.11.1), [11](#2Sam.11.11)). His character is deeply stained by the part he willingly took in the murder of Uriah (11:14-25). He acted apparently from a sense of duty in putting Absalom to death (18:1-14). David was unmindful of the many services Joab had rendered to him, and afterwards gave the command of the army to Amasa, Joab’s cousin ([2 Sam. 20:1-13](#2Sam.20.1); [19:13](#2Sam.19.13)). When David was dying Joab espoused the cause of Adonijah in preference to that of Solomon. He was afterwards slain by Benaiah, by the command of Solomon, in accordance with his father’s injunction ([2 Sam. 3:29](#2Sam.3.29); [20:5-13](#2Sam.20.5)), at the altar to which he had fled for refuge. Thus this hoary conspirator died without one to lift up a voice in his favour. He was buried in his own property in the “wilderness,” probably in the north-east of Jerusalem ([1 Kings 2:5](#1Kgs.2.5), [28](#1Kgs.2.28)-34). Benaiah succeeded him as commander-in-chief of the army.
The son of Asaph, and “recorder” (q.v.) or chronicler to King Hezekiah ([2 Kings 18:18](#2Kgs.18.18), [26](#2Kgs.18.26), [37](#2Kgs.18.37)).
One of the sons of Obed-edom ([1 Chr. 26:4](#1Chr.26.4)), a Korhite porter.
Son of Joahaz, and “recorder” (q.v.) or keeper of the state archives under King Josiah ([2 Chr. 34:8](#2Chr.34.8)).
([2 Chr. 34:8](#2Chr.34.8)), a contracted form of Jehoahaz (q.v.).

The wife of Chuza, the steward of Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee ([Luke 8:3](#Luke.8.3)). She was one of the women who ministered to our Lord, and to whom he appeared after his resurrection ([Luke 8:3](#Luke.8.3); [24:10](#Luke.24.10)).
The grandson of Zerubbabel, in the lineage of Christ ([Luke 3:27](#Luke.3.27)); the same as Hananiah ([1 Chr. 3:19](#1Chr.3.19)).

The son and successor of Jehoahaz, king of Israel ([2 Kings 14:1](#2Kgs.14.1); comp. 12:1; 13:10). When he ascended the throne the kingdom was suffering from the invasion of the Syrians. Hazael “was cutting Israel short.” He tolerated the worship of the golden calves, yet seems to have manifested a character of sincere devotion to the God of his fathers. …

The son of King Ahaziah. While yet an infant, he was saved from the general massacre of the family by his aunt Jehosheba, and was apparently the only surviving descendant of Solomon ([2 Chr. 21:4](#2Chr.21.4), [17](#2Chr.21.17)). His uncle, the high priest Jehoiada, brought him forth to public notice when he was eight years of age, and crowned and anointed him king of Judah with the usual ceremonies. …
A contracted form of Jehoash, the father of Gideon ([Judg. 6:11](#Judg.6.11), [29](#Judg.6.29); 8:13, 29, 32).
One of King Ahab’s sons ([1 Kings 22:26](#1Kgs.22.26)).
One of the Benjamite archers who joined David at Ziklag ([1 Chr. 12:3](#1Chr.12.3)).
One who had charge of the royal stores of oil under David and Solomon ([1 Chr. 27:28](#1Chr.27.28)).

Persecuted, an Arabian patriarch who resided in the land of Uz (q.v.). While living in the midst of great prosperity, he was suddenly overwhelmed by a series of sore trials that fell upon him. Amid all his sufferings he maintained his integrity. Once more God visited him with the rich tokens of his goodness and even greater prosperity than he had enjoyed before. He survived the period of trial for one hundred and forty years, and died in a good old age, an example to succeeding generations of integrity ([Ezek. 14:14](#Ezek.14.14), [20](#Ezek.14.20)) and of submissive patience under the sorest calamities ([James 5:11](#Jas.5.11)). His history, so far as it is known, is recorded in his book.
One of the sons of Joktan, and founder of an Arabian tribe ([Gen. 10:29](#Gen.10.29)).
A Canaanitish king ([Josh. 11:1](#Josh.11.1)) who joined the confederacy against Joshua.

Jehovah is her glory, the wife of Amram, and the mother of Miriam, Aaron, and Moses ([Num. 26:59](#Num.26.59)). She is spoken of as the sister of Kohath, Amram’s father ([Ex. 6:20](#Exod.6.20); comp. 16, 18; 2:1-10).
The oldest of Samuel’s two sons appointed by him as judges in Beersheba ([1 Sam. 8:2](#1Sam.8.2)).
A Levite of the family of Gershom ([1 Chr. 15:7](#1Chr.15.7), [11](#1Chr.15.11)).
The second of the twelve minor prophets. He was the son of Pethuel. His personal history is only known from his book.
One of David’s famous warriors ([1 Chr. 11:38](#1Chr.11.38)).
A Benjamite who joined David at Ziklag ([1 Chr. 12:7](#1Chr.12.7)).
Jehovah is his help, one of the Korhites who became part of David’s body-guard ([1 Chr. 12:6](#1Chr.12.6)).

Son of Careah, one of the Jewish chiefs who rallied round Gedaliah, whom Nebuchadnezzar had made governor in Jerusalem ([2 Kings 25:23](#2Kgs.25.23); [Jer. 40:8](#Jer.40.8)). He warned Gedaliah of the plans of Ishmael against him, a warning which was unheeded ([Jer. 40:13](#Jer.40.13), [16](#Jer.40.16)). He afterwards pursued the murderer of the governor, and rescued the captives (41:8, 13, 15, 16). He and his associates subsequently fled to Tahpanhes in Egypt (43:2, 4, 5), taking Jeremiah with them. “The flight of Gedaliah’s community to Egypt extinguished the last remaining spark of life in the Jewish state. The work of the ten centuries since Joshua crossed the Jordan had been undone.”
The oldest of King Josiah’s sons ([1 Chr. 3:15](#1Chr.3.15)).
One of the Gadite heroes who joined David in the desert of Judah ([1 Chr. 12:12](#1Chr.12.12)).

The “forerunner of our Lord.” We have but fragmentary and imperfect accounts of him in the Gospels. He was of priestly descent. His father, Zacharias, was a priest of the course of Abia ([1 Chr. 24:10](#1Chr.24.10)), and his mother, Elisabeth, was of the daughters of Aaron ([Luke 1:5](#Luke.1.5)). The mission of John was the subject of prophecy ([Matt. 3:3](#Matt.3.3); [Isa. 40:3](#Isa.40.3); [Mal. 3:1](#Mal.3.1)). His birth, which took place six months before that of Jesus, was foretold by an angel. …

THE APOSTLE, brother of James the “Greater” ([Matt. 4:21](#Matt.4.21); [10:2](#Matt.10.2); [Mark 1:19](#Mark.1.19); [3:17](#Mark.3.17); [10:35](#Mark.10.35)). He was one, probably the younger, of the sons of Zebedee ([Matt. 4:21](#Matt.4.21)) and Salome ([Matt. 27:56](#Matt.27.56); comp. [Mark 15:40](#Mark.15.40)), and was born at Bethsaida. His father was apparently a man of some wealth (comp. [Mark 1:20](#Mark.1.20); [Luke 5:3](#Luke.5.3); [John 19:27](#John.19.27)). He was doubtless trained in all that constituted the ordinary education of Jewish youth. When he grew up he followed the occupation of a fisherman on the Lake of Galilee. …

The evangelist; “John whose surname was Mark” ([Acts 12:12](#Acts.12.12), [25](#Acts.12.25)). Mark (Marcus, [Col. 4:10](#Col.4.10), etc.) was his Roman name, which gradually came to supersede his Jewish name John. He is called John in [Acts 13:5](#Acts.13.5), [13](#Acts.13.13), and Mark in 15:39, [2 Tim. 4:11](#2Tim.4.11), etc.
One who, with Annas and Caiaphas, sat in judgment on the apostles Peter and John ([Acts 4:6](#Acts.4.6)). He was of the kindred of the high priest; otherwise unknown.
(whom Jehovah has set up) = Jehoiakim, a high priest, the son and successor of Jeshua ([Neh. 12:10](#Neh.12.10), [12](#Neh.12.12), [26](#Neh.12.26)).
The founder of one of the courses of the priests ([Neh. 11:10](#Neh.11.10)).
[Ezra 8:16](#Ezra.8.16), a “man of understanding” whom Ezra sent to “bring ministers for the house of God.”
Whom Jehovah has set up, one of the descendants of Shelah ([1 Chr. 4:22](#1Chr.4.22)).
Snarer, the second son of Abraham and Keturah ([Gen. 25:2](#Gen.25.2), [3](#Gen.25.3); [1 Chr. 1:32](#1Chr.1.32)).

Little, the second of the two sons of Eber ([Gen. 10:25](#Gen.10.25); [1 Chr. 1:19](#1Chr.1.19)). There is an Arab tradition that Joktan (Arab. Kahtan) was the progenitor of all the purest tribes of Central and Southern Arabia.

A son of Rechab, the founder of a tribe who bound themselves by a vow to abstain from wine ([Jer. 35:6-19](#Jer.35.6)). There were different settlements of Rechabites ([Judg. 1:16](#Judg.1.16); [4:11](#Judg.4.11); [1 Chr. 2:55](#1Chr.2.55)). His interview and alliance with Jehu are mentioned in [2 Kings 10:15-23](#2Kgs.10.15). He went with Jehu in his chariot to Samaria.
Son of Shammah, and David’s nephew, and also one of his chief warriors ([2 Sam. 21:21](#2Sam.21.21)). He slew a giant in Gath.

A dove, the son of Amittai of Gath-hepher. He was a prophet of Israel, and predicted the restoration of the ancient boundaries ([2 Kings 14:25-27](#2Kgs.14.25)) of the kingdom. He exercised his ministry very early in the reign of Jeroboam II., and thus was contemporary with Hosea and Amos; or possibly he preceded them, and consequently may have been the very oldest of all the prophets whose writings we possess. His personal history is mainly to be gathered from the book which bears his name. It is chiefly interesting from the two-fold character in which he appears, (1) as a missionary to heathen Nineveh, and (2) as a type of the “Son of man.”
The father of the apostles Peter ([John 21:15-17](#John.21.15)) and Andrew; but the reading should be (also in 1:42), as in the Revised Version, “John,” instead of Jonas.

The eldest son of king Saul, and the bosom friend of David. He is first mentioned when he was about thirty years of age, some time after his father’s accession to the throne ([1 Sam. 13:2](#1Sam.13.2)). Like his father, he was a man of great strength and activity ([2 Sam. 1:23](#2Sam.1.23)), and excelled in archery and slinging ([1 Chr. 12:2](#1Chr.12.2);[2 Sam. 1:22](#2Sam.1.22)). The affection that evidently subsisted between him and his father was interrupted by the growth of Saul’s insanity. …

Son of the high priest Abiathar, and one who adhered to David at the time of Absalom’s rebellion ([2 Sam. 15:27](#2Sam.15.27), [36](#2Sam.15.36)). He is the last descendant of Eli of whom there is any record.

A Levite descended from Gershom ([Judg. 18:30](#Judg.18.30)). His history is recorded in 17:7-13 and 18:30. The Rabbins changed this name into Manasseh “to screen the memory of the great lawgiver from the stain of having so unworthy an apostate among his near descendants.” He became priest of the idol image at Dan, and this office continued in his family till the Captivity.

The son of Ahab and Jezebel, and successor to his brother Ahaziah on the throne of Israel. He reigned twelve years, B.C. 896-884 ([2 Kings 1:17](#2Kgs.1.17); [3:1](#2Kgs.3.1)). His first work was to reduce to subjection the Moabites, who had asserted their independence in the reign of his brother. Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, assisted Jehoram in this effort. He was further helped by his ally the king of Edom. Elisha went forth with the confederated army ([2 Kings 3:1-19](#2Kgs.3.1)), and at the solicitation of Jehoshaphat encouraged the army with the assurance from the Lord of a speedy victory. The Moabites under Mesha their king were utterly routed and their cities destroyed. …
The son of Tou, king of Hamath, sent by his father to congratulate David on his victory over Hadarezer, king of Syria ([1 Chr. 18:10](#1Chr.18.10); called Joram [2 Sam. 8:10](#2Sam.8.10)).
One of the Benjamite archers who joined David at Ziklag ([1 Chr. 12:4](#1Chr.12.4)).

Jehovah-justified, the son of the high priest Seraiah at the time of the Babylonian exile ([1 Chr. 6:14](#1Chr.6.14), [15](#1Chr.6.15)). He was carried into captivity by Nebuchadnezzar, and probably died in Babylon. He was the father of Jeshua, or Joshua, who returned with Zerubbabel.

The elder of the two sons of Jacob by Rachel ([Gen. 30:23](#Gen.30.23), [24](#Gen.30.24)), who, on the occasion of his birth, said, “God hath taken away [Heb. ‘asaph] my reproach.” “The Lord shall add [Heb. yoseph] to me another son” ([Gen. 30:24](#Gen.30.24)). He was a child of probably six years of age when his father returned from Haran to Canaan and took up his residence in the old patriarchal town of Hebron. “Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age,” and he “made him a long garment with sleeves” ([Gen. 37:3](#Gen.37.3), R.V. marg.), i.e., a garment long and full, such as was worn by the children of nobles. …

The foster-father of our Lord ([Matt. 1:16](#Matt.1.16); [Luke 3:23](#Luke.3.23)). He lived at Nazareth in Galilee ([Luke 2:4](#Luke.2.4)). He is called a “just man.” He was by trade a carpenter ([Matt. 13:55](#Matt.13.55)). He is last mentioned in connection with the journey to Jerusalem, when Jesus was twelve years old. It is probable that he died before Jesus entered on his public ministry. This is concluded from the fact that Mary only was present at the marriage feast in Cana of Galilee. His name does not appear in connection with the scenes of the crucifixion along with that of Mary (q.v.), [John 19:25](#John.19.25).

A native of Arimathea, probably the Ramah of the Old Testament ([1 Sam. 1:19](#1Sam.1.19)), a man of wealth, and a member of the Sanhedrim ([Matt. 27:57](#Matt.27.57); [Luke 23:50](#Luke.23.50)), an “honourable counsellor, who waited for the kingdom of God.” As soon as he heard the tidings of Christ’s death, he “went in boldly” (lit. “having summoned courage, he went”) “unto Pilate, and craved the body of Jesus.” Pilate having ascertained from the centurion that the death had really taken place, granted Joseph’s request, who immediately, having purchased fine linen ([Mark 15:46](#Mark.15.46)), proceeded to Golgotha to take the body down from the cross. …
One of the sons of Asaph, head of the first division of sacred musicians ([1 Chr. 25:2](#1Chr.25.2), [9](#1Chr.25.9)).
The son of Judah, and father of Semei ([Luke 3:26](#Luke.3.26)). Other two of the same name in the ancestry of Christ are also mentioned (3:24, 30).

Jehovah is his help, or Jehovah the Saviour. The son of Nun, of the tribe of Ephraim, the successor of Moses as the leader of Israel. He is called Jehoshua in [Num. 13:16](#Num.13.16) (A.V.), and Jesus in [Acts 7:45](#Acts.7.45) and [Heb. 4:8](#Heb.4.8) (R.V., Joshua).
Healed by Jehovah, or Jehovah will support. …

Common in later times among the Jews in Palestine ([Matt. 23:37](#Matt.23.37); [Luke 13:34](#Luke.13.34)). It is noticeable that this familiar bird is only mentioned in these passages in connection with our Lord’s lamentation over the impenitence of Jerusalem.

The son and successor of Uzziah on the throne of Judah. As during his last years Uzziah was excluded from public life on account of his leprosy, his son, then twenty-five years of age, administered for seven years the affairs of the kingdom in his father’s stead ([2 Chr. 26:21](#2Chr.26.21), [23](#2Chr.26.23); 27:1). After his father’s death he became sole monarch, and reigned for sixteen years (B.C. 759-743). He ruled in the fear of God, and his reign was prosperous. He was contemporary with the prophets Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah, by whose ministrations he profited. He was buried in the sepulchre of the kings, greatly lamented by the people ([2 Kings 15:38](#2Kgs.15.38); [2 Chr. 27:7-9](#2Chr.27.7)).

The youngest of Gideon’s seventy sons. He escaped when the rest were put to death by the order of Abimelech ([Judg. 9:5](#Judg.9.5)). When “the citizens of Shechem and the whole house of Millo” were gathered together “by the plain of the pillar” (i.e., the stone set up by Joshua, 24:26; comp. [Gen. 35:4](#Gen.35.4)) “that was in Shechem, to make Abimelech king,” from one of the heights of Mount Gerizim he protested against their doing so in the earliest parable, that of the bramble-king. His words then spoken were prophetic. …

Jubilee, music, Lamech’s second son by Adah, of the line of Cain. He was the inventor of “the harp” (Heb. kinnor, properly “lyre”) and “the organ” (Heb. ‘ugab, properly “mouth-organ” or Pan’s pipe), [Gen. 4:21](#Gen.4.21).

Able, the son of Shelemiah. He is also called Jucal ([Jer. 38:1](#Jer.38.1)). He was one of the two persons whom Zedekiah sent to request the prophet Jeremiah to pray for the kingdom ([Jer. 37:3](#Jer.37.3)) during the time of its final siege by Nebuchadnezzar. He was accompanied by Zephaniah (q.v.).
The father of Simeon in Christ’s maternal ancestry ([Luke 3:30](#Luke.3.30)).

Praise, the fourth son of Jacob by Leah. The name originated in Leah’s words of praise to the Lord on account of his birth: “Now will I praise [Heb. odeh] Jehovah, and she called his name Yehudah” ([Gen. 29:35](#Gen.29.35)).

Son of Simon ([John 6:71](#John.6.71); [13:2](#John.13.2), [26](#John.13.26)), surnamed Iscariot, i.e., a man of Kerioth ([Josh. 15:25](#Josh.15.25)). His name is uniformly the last in the list of the apostles, as given in the synoptic (i.e., the first three) Gospels. …

A Christian teacher, surnamed Barsabas. He was sent from Jerusalem to Antioch along with Paul and Barnabas with the decision of the council ([Acts 15:22](#Acts.15.22), [27](#Acts.15.27), [32](#Acts.15.32)). He was a “prophet” and a “chief man among the brethren.”

A Jew of Damascus ([Acts 9:11](#Acts.9.11)), to whose house Ananias was sent. The street called “Straight” in which it was situated is identified with the modern “street of bazaars,” where is still pointed out the so-called “house of Judas.”

'= Judas. Among the apostles there were two who bore this name, (1) Judas ([Jude 1](#Jude.1.1):1; [Matt. 13:55](#Matt.13.55); [John 14:22](#John.14.22); [Acts 1:13](#Acts.1.13)), called also Lebbaeus or Thaddaeus ([Matt. 10:3](#Matt.10.3); [Mark 3:18](#Mark.3.18)); and (2) Judas Iscariot ([Matt. 10:4](#Matt.10.4); [Mark 3:19](#Mark.3.19)). He who is called “the brother of James” ([Luke 6:16](#Luke.6.16)), may be the same with the Judas surnamed Lebbaeus. The only thing recorded regarding him is in [John 14:22](#John.14.22).
A Christian woman at Rome to whom Paul sent his salutations ([Rom. 16:15](#Rom.16.15)), supposed to be the wife of Philologus.

The centurion of the Augustan cohort, or the emperor’s body-guard, in whose charge Paul was sent prisoner to Rome ([Acts 27:1](#Acts.27.1), [3](#Acts.27.3), [43](#Acts.27.43)). He entreated Paul “courteously,” showing in many ways a friendly regard for him.
([Rom. 16:7](#Rom.16.7)), a Christian at Rome to whom Paul sends salutations along with Andronicus.
A Jewish proselyte at Corinth, in whose house, next door to the synagogue, Paul held meetings and preached after he left the synagogue ([Acts 18:7](#Acts.18.7)).
Before God; i.e., his servant, one of the Levites who returned with Zerubbabel from the Captivity ([Neh. 9:4](#Neh.9.4); [10:9](#Neh.10.9); [12:8](#Neh.12.8)).
Bald, the father of Johanan and Jonathan, who for a time were loyal to Gedaliah, the Babylonian governor of Jerusalem ([Jer. 40:8](#Jer.40.8), [13](#Jer.40.13), [15](#Jer.40.15), [16](#Jer.40.16)).
Dark-skinned, the second son of Ishmael ([Gen. 25:13](#Gen.25.13)).
Eastward, the last-named of the sons of Ishmael ([Gen. 25:15](#Gen.25.15)).
Dwarf, a Levite who assisted Ezra in expounding the law to the people ([Neh. 8:7](#Neh.8.7); [10:10](#Neh.10.10)).
Son of Shiphtan, appointed on behalf of the tribe of Ephraim to partition the land of Canaan ([Num. 34:24](#Num.34.24)).

Caleb’s younger brother, and father of Othniel ([Josh. 15:17](#Josh.15.17)), whose family was of importance in Israel down to the time of David ([1 Chr. 27:15](#1Chr.27.15)). Some think that Othniel ([Judg. 1:13](#Judg.1.13)), and not Kenaz, was Caleb’s brother.
Horn of the face-paint = cosmetic-box, the name of Job’s third daughter ([Job. 42:14](#Job.42.14)), born after prosperity had returned to him.

Incense, the wife of Abraham, whom he married probably after Sarah’s death ([Gen. 25:1-6](#Gen.25.1)), by whom he had six sons, whom he sent away into the east country. Her nationality is unknown. She is styled “Abraham’s concubine” ([1 Chr. 1:32](#1Chr.1.32)). Through the offshoots of the Keturah line Abraham became the “father of many nations.”

A Benjamite, the son of Abiel, and father of king Saul ([1 Sam. 9:1](#1Sam.9.1), [3](#1Sam.9.3); [10:11](#1Sam.10.11), [21](#1Sam.10.21); [14:51](#1Sam.14.51); [2 Sam. 21:14](#2Sam.21.14)). All that is recorded of him is that he sent his son Saul in search of his asses that had strayed, and that he was buried in Zelah. Called Cis, [Acts 13:21](#Acts.13.21) (R.V., Kish).
A Levite of the family of Merari ([1 Chr. 23:21](#1Chr.23.21); [24:29](#1Chr.24.29)).
A Levite in the time of Hezekiah ([2 Chr. 29:12](#2Chr.29.12)).

Assembly, the second son of Levi, and father of Amram ([Gen. 46:11](#Gen.46.11)). He came down to Egypt with Jacob, and lived to the age of one hundred and thirty-three years ([Ex. 6:18](#Exod.6.18)).

A Levite, the son of Izhar, the brother of Amram, the father of Moses and Aaron ([Ex. 6:21](#Exod.6.21)). The institution of the Aaronic priesthood and the Levitical service at Sinai was a great religious revolution. The old priesthood of the heads of families passed away. This gave rise to murmurings and discontent, while the Israelites were encamped at Kadesh for the first time, which came to a head in a rebellion against Moses and Aaron, headed by Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. Two hundred and fifty princes, “men of renown” i.e., well-known men from among the other tribes, joined this conspiracy. …
The third son of Esau, by Aholibamah ([Gen. 36:14](#Gen.36.14); [1 Chr. 1:35](#1Chr.1.35)).
A Levite and temple-warder of the Korahites, the son of Asaph. He was father of Shallum and Meshelemiah, temple-porters ([1 Chr. 9:19](#1Chr.9.19); [26:1](#1Chr.26.1)).
A Levitical porter at the east gate of the temple ([2 Chr. 31:14](#2Chr.31.14)).
White, one of the two sons of Gershon, the son of Levi ([Ex. 6:17](#Exod.6.17); [Num. 3:18](#Num.3.18), [21](#Num.3.21)).

The son of Bethuel, who was the son of Nahor, Abraham’s brother. He lived at Haran in Mesopotamia. His sister Rebekah was Isaac’s wife ([Gen. 24](#Gen.24)). Jacob, one of the sons of this marriage, fled to the house of Laban, whose daughters Leah and Rachel (ch. 29) he eventually married.
